title: main()
body:
Every C++ program has **exactly one** `main()`, it is where execution starts, and it returns
`int`.

```c++
int main() {
	// ...
	return 0;      // 0 means success
}
```

`return 0` is the exit status handed back to the [[Shell]], not to anything in your program.
Zero is success and anything else is a failure code, which is what lets a script tell whether
your program worked. Nothing in the language stops you writing `void main()`; it is wrong and
some compilers reject it.

`main()` solves the main problem and calls [[Function]]s to solve the sub-problems. That
division is the whole of [[Program design]]: `main()` should read like the [[Structure chart]],
mostly calls and almost no detail. A `main()` two hundred lines long is a design that never
happened.

Two things `main()` anchors:

- **Top-down testing** starts here and needs stubs for the functions that do not exist yet.
  Bottom-up testing starts at the leaves and needs a [[Driver]], which is itself a throwaway
  `main()`. See [[debugging]].
- A [[Client Program]] is a `main()` that uses somebody else's [[Class]] through its
  [[Interface]].

Nothing in `main()` is special to the compiler beyond the name. What actually starts the
program, sets up the stack, and calls it is the loader; see [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]].
